title: Feature scaling: making every feature count
summary: Standardize features with statistics learned from the training data, so a model's answer doesn't depend on units.

sources.section: 10.6 Key Steps of PCA in Practice

license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner

steps.title: Centimetres or millimetres?
steps.body:
In the capstone, the nearest-centroid classifier measured distance using plant height and leaf size.
Heights spread over about 20 cm, leaves over about 2 cm, so height decided almost everything. Worse:
write the heights in millimetres instead and the distances change, and so can the predictions. The
plants are the same; only the unit changed. A model whose answer depends on the unit you chose is
not measuring what you meant.

steps.title: Measure every feature in its own spread
steps.body:
Instead of raw units, describe each value by how far it is from that feature's average, counted in
standard deviations. A height 1 standard deviation above average and a leaf 1 standard deviation
above average now count the same. This is **standardization**, and the result has no units. The
averages and spreads are learned from the **training** data, then applied unchanged to every new
example, exactly like a model's parameters.

questions: What is the standardized value of a training example that is exactly average?
If you computed the averages from the test rows too, which habit from the capstone would you break?

steps.title: Watch one column being standardized
steps.body: The mean 20 and standard deviation 10 were learned earlier from a training set; here they scale three new values (whose own spread is different). Each frame shows the variables just before the highlighted line runs; the last frame shows what that line printed.

frames.note: Scale three new values with the training mean 20 and standard deviation 10.
One below average, exactly average, one above.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Standardization:** for each feature `d`, compute the mean `μ_d` and standard deviation `σ_d` over
the training examples, then replace every value `x_d` by `z_d = (x_d − μ_d) / σ_d`. The standardized
training data has mean 0 in every feature and standard deviation 1 in every non-constant feature,
and no units.

**With NumPy:** `X.mean(axis=0)` and `X.std(axis=0)` give one mean and one standard deviation per
column (`np.std` divides by `N` unless you pass `ddof=1`); `(X - means) / stds` broadcasts them
across every row.

**A constant feature** has `σ_d = 0`, and dividing by 0 is undefined. This lesson uses 1 instead,
so such a column becomes all zeros: it carries no information to tell examples apart.

**Fit on training data only:** `μ` and `σ` are learned parameters. Compute them from the training
rows and reuse them for test rows and new examples. Computing them from test rows leaks information;
computing them from a single new example gives a spread of 0 and throws away the training reference.

steps.title: Run it: same plant, different units
steps.body:
The same training plants and the same new plant, with heights in centimetres and then millimetres.
Predict which of the four answers change.
steps.code:
import numpy as np

X = [[12.0, 3.1], [14.5, 2.8], [13.3, 3.6], [16.8, 4.4], [30.2, 4.5], [28.4, 5.1], [26.0, 4.2], [22.5, 5.0]]
y = ['fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm']
new = [20.6, 2.5]

def nearest(X, y, x):
    X, x = np.array(X), np.array(x)
    cents = {c: X[[i for i in range(len(y)) if y[i] == c]].mean(axis=0) for c in sorted(set(y))}
    return min(cents, key=lambda c: np.sum((x - cents[c]) ** 2))

def scaled(X, x):
    X = np.array(X)
    m, s = X.mean(axis=0), X.std(axis=0)
    return (X - m) / s, (np.array(x) - m) / s

X_mm = [[h * 10, leaf] for h, leaf in X]
new_mm = [new[0] * 10, new[1]]
print('raw, cm:', nearest(X, y, new))
print('raw, mm:', nearest(X_mm, y, new_mm))
Z, z = scaled(X, new)
print('scaled, cm:', nearest(Z, y, z))
Z_mm, z_mm = scaled(X_mm, new_mm)
print('scaled, mm:', nearest(Z_mm, y, z_mm))
steps.expected_output:
raw, cm: fern
raw, mm: palm
scaled, cm: fern
scaled, mm: fern

steps.title: Your turn: standardize train and test
steps.body:
Complete `standardize(X_train, X_test)`. Learn each column's mean and standard deviation (dividing
by `N`) from `X_train` only; use 1 for any column whose standard deviation is 0. Return the
standardized training and test sets as two lists of lists of floats. Raise `ValueError` if
`X_train` has no rows; `X_test` may be empty. Don't change the inputs.
hints: `A.mean(axis=0)` and `A.std(axis=0)` give one value per column; compute them from the training array only.
`stds[stds == 0] = 1.0` replaces zero spreads; `np.array(X_test, dtype=float).reshape(-1, A.shape[1])` copes with an empty test set.

tests.name: each column on its own scale
tests.code:
tr, te = standardize([[1, 10], [3, 30]], [[2, 40]])
assert tr == [[-1.0, -1.0], [1.0, 1.0]], f'column means 2 and 20, spreads 1 and 10; got {tr}'
assert te == [[0.0, 2.0]], f'scale test rows with the training statistics; got {te}'

tests.name: test rows never change the statistics
tests.code:
tr, te = standardize([[0, 4], [2, 8]], [[5, 0], [100, 100]])
assert tr == [[-1.0, -1.0], [1.0, 1.0]], f'got {tr}'
assert te == [[4.0, -3.0], [99.0, 47.0]], f'means 1 and 6, spreads 1 and 2, from the training rows only; got {te}'

tests.name: divide by N, not N - 1
tests.code:
tr, te = standardize([[0], [1], [2]], [[3]])
sd = (2 / 3) ** 0.5
assert all(abs(a[0] - b) < 1e-12 for a, b in zip(tr, [-1 / sd, 0.0, 1 / sd])), f'the spread is sqrt(2/3), as np.std gives by default; got {tr}'
assert abs(te[0][0] - 2 / sd) < 1e-12, f'got {te}'

tests.name: a constant column becomes zeros
tests.code:
tr, te = standardize([[5, 1], [5, 3]], [[7, 2]])
assert tr == [[0.0, -1.0], [0.0, 1.0]], f'the first column has spread 0: divide by 1 instead; got {tr}'
assert te == [[2.0, 0.0]], f'got {te}'

tests.name: three features, unrounded
tests.code:
tr, te = standardize([[1, 0, 0.5], [2, 0, 0.25], [6, 0, 1.0]], [[3, 9, 0.6]])
import statistics
cols = [[1, 2, 6], [0, 0, 0], [0.5, 0.25, 1.0]]
m = [statistics.fmean(c) for c in cols]
s = [statistics.pstdev(c) or 1.0 for c in cols]
z = lambda row: [(v - m[j]) / s[j] for j, v in enumerate(row)]
want_tr, want_te = [z(r) for r in [[1, 0, 0.5], [2, 0, 0.25], [6, 0, 1.0]]], [z([3, 9, 0.6])]
assert [len(r) for r in tr] == [3, 3, 3] and [len(r) for r in te] == [3], f'one row out per row in, three values each; got {tr}, {te}'
assert all(abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for got, want in ((tr, want_tr), (te, want_te)) for gr, wr in zip(got, want) for a, b in zip(gr, wr)), f'expected about {want_tr} and {want_te}; got {tr} and {te}'

tests.name: a single training row
tests.code:
tr, te = standardize([[3, 4]], [[5, 4], [3, 0]])
assert tr == [[0.0, 0.0]] and te == [[2.0, 0.0], [0.0, -4.0]], f'one training row: every spread is 0, so divide by 1; got {tr}, {te}'

tests.name: a tiny spread is still a spread
tests.code:
tr, te = standardize([[1e-12, 5], [2e-12, 5], [3e-12, 7]], [[4e-12, 6]])
import statistics
cols = [[1e-12, 2e-12, 3e-12], [5, 5, 7]]
m = [statistics.fmean(c) for c in cols]
s = [statistics.pstdev(c) for c in cols]
z = lambda row: [(v - m[j]) / s[j] for j, v in enumerate(row)]
want_tr, want_te = [z(r) for r in [[1e-12, 5], [2e-12, 5], [3e-12, 7]]], [z([4e-12, 6])]
assert all(abs(a - b) < 1e-9 for got, want in ((tr, want_tr), (te, want_te)) for gr, wr in zip(got, want) for a, b in zip(gr, wr)), f'a spread of about 8e-13 is not 0: only an exactly constant column is divided by 1; expected about {want_tr} and {want_te}, got {tr} and {te}'

tests.name: an empty test set is fine
tests.code:
tr, te = standardize([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [])
assert te == [], f'got {te}'
assert tr == [[-1.0, -1.0], [1.0, 1.0]]

tests.name: plain lists of floats
tests.code:
tr, te = standardize([[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[2, 3]])
assert type(tr) is list and type(te) is list and all(type(r) is list for r in tr + te), 'return lists of lists'
assert all(isinstance(v, float) for r in tr + te for v in r), 'every value is a float'

tests.name: inputs are not changed, rows stay in order
tests.code:
import copy
a, b = [[5, 1], [1, 3], [3, 8]], [[4, 0], [0, 9], [2, 2]]
keep_a, keep_b = copy.deepcopy(a), copy.deepcopy(b)
tr, te = standardize(a, b)
assert a == keep_a and b == keep_b, 'do not modify X_train or X_test'
import statistics
m = [3.0, 4.0]
s = [statistics.pstdev([5, 1, 3]), statistics.pstdev([1, 3, 8])]
z = lambda r: [(r[j] - m[j]) / s[j] for j in range(2)]
for got, rows in ((tr, keep_a), (te, keep_b)):
    assert len(got) == 3 and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-12 for g, r in zip(got, rows) for x, y in zip(g, z(r))), f'one output row per input row, in the same order; got {got}'

tests.name: no training rows

steps.title: Challenge: a classifier that ignores units
steps.body:
The starter gives you `fit_centroids` and `predict_centroids`. Write two functions.
`fit_scaled_centroids(X, y)` learns each column's mean and standard deviation (dividing by `N`,
with 1 for a zero spread) from `X`, standardizes `X`, fits centroids to the standardized rows, and
returns `{'means': [...], 'stds': [...], 'centroids': {...}}` with plain lists of floats. Raise
`ValueError` if `X` is empty or its length differs from `y`.
`predict_scaled(model, X)` standardizes the new rows with the model's **stored** means and standard
deviations and returns the nearest centroid's label for each row (it must work for a single row,
and return `[]` for no rows);
equally near centroids go to the label first in sorted order, as `predict_centroids` does.
hints: Inside `fit_scaled_centroids`, compute `Z = (X - means) / stds` and call `fit_centroids(Z, y)`.
In `predict_scaled`, never compute a mean or spread from the rows you are predicting: use `model['means']` and `model['stds']`.

tests.name: the learned statistics
tests.code:
X = [[12.0, 3.1], [14.5, 2.8], [13.3, 3.6], [16.8, 4.4], [30.2, 4.5], [28.4, 5.1], [26.0, 4.2], [22.5, 5.0]]
y = ['fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm']
model = fit_scaled_centroids(X, y)
import statistics
want_m = [statistics.fmean(r[j] for r in X) for j in range(2)]
want_s = [statistics.pstdev([r[j] for r in X]) for j in range(2)]
assert all(abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for a, b in zip(model['means'], want_m)), f'column means of X; got {model["means"]}'
assert all(abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for a, b in zip(model['stds'], want_s)), f'spreads dividing by N; got {model["stds"]}'
assert sorted(model['centroids']) == ['fern', 'palm']
for label, rows in (('fern', X[:4]), ('palm', X[4:])):
    want = [(statistics.fmean(r[j] for r in rows) - want_m[j]) / want_s[j] for j in range(2)]
    got = model['centroids'][label]
    assert len(got) == 2 and all(abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for a, b in zip(got, want)), f'the {label} centroid is the mean of its standardized rows, about {want}; got {got}'

tests.name: classes of different sizes
tests.code:
X = [[0, 1], [2, 3], [4, 8], [10, 0], [12, 2]]
y = ['a', 'a', 'a', 'b', 'b']
import statistics
m = [statistics.fmean(r[j] for r in X) for j in range(2)]
s = [statistics.pstdev([r[j] for r in X]) for j in range(2)]
Z = [[(r[j] - m[j]) / s[j] for j in range(2)] for r in X]
model = fit_scaled_centroids(X, y)
for label, rows in (('a', Z[:3]), ('b', Z[3:])):
    want = [statistics.fmean(r[j] for r in rows) for j in range(2)]
    got = model['centroids'][label]
    assert len(got) == 2 and all(abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for a, b in zip(got, want)), f'{label} has {len(rows)} rows: its centroid is their mean, about {want}; got {got}'

tests.name: interleaved labels
tests.code:
X = [[0, 1], [10, 0], [2, 3], [12, 2], [4, 8]]
y = ['a', 'b', 'a', 'b', 'a']
import statistics
m = [statistics.fmean(r[j] for r in X) for j in range(2)]
s = [statistics.pstdev([r[j] for r in X]) for j in range(2)]
Z = [[(r[j] - m[j]) / s[j] for j in range(2)] for r in X]
model = fit_scaled_centroids(X, y)
for label, rows in (('a', [Z[0], Z[2], Z[4]]), ('b', [Z[1], Z[3]])):
    want = [statistics.fmean(r[j] for r in rows) for j in range(2)]
    got = model['centroids'][label]
    assert len(got) == 2 and all(abs(a - b) < 1e-12 for a, b in zip(got, want)), f'the {label} rows are not next to each other: its centroid is about {want}; got {got}'
assert predict_scaled(model, [[1, 2], [11, 1], [3, 6]]) == ['a', 'b', 'a']

tests.name: a single training row
tests.code:
model = fit_scaled_centroids([[3, 4]], ['a'])
assert model == {'means': [3.0, 4.0], 'stds': [1.0, 1.0], 'centroids': {'a': [0.0, 0.0]}}, f'got {model}'
assert predict_scaled(model, [[10, 10], [3, 4]]) == ['a', 'a']

tests.name: plain lists of floats
tests.code:
X = [[12.0, 3.1], [14.5, 2.8], [13.3, 3.6], [16.8, 4.4], [30.2, 4.5], [28.4, 5.1], [26.0, 4.2], [22.5, 5.0]]
y = ['fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm']
model = fit_scaled_centroids(X, y)
assert set(model) == {'means', 'stds', 'centroids'}, f'keys means, stds, centroids; got {sorted(model)}'
for v in [model['means'], model['stds'], *model['centroids'].values()]:
    assert type(v) is list and all(isinstance(t, float) for t in v), f'plain lists of floats; got {v!r}'

tests.name: units don't matter
tests.code:
X = [[12.0, 3.1], [14.5, 2.8], [13.3, 3.6], [16.8, 4.4], [30.2, 4.5], [28.4, 5.1], [26.0, 4.2], [22.5, 5.0]]
y = ['fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm']
new = [[20.6, 2.5], [15.0, 5.2], [27.0, 3.0], [21.0, 4.0]]
cm = predict_scaled(fit_scaled_centroids(X, y), new)
mm = predict_scaled(fit_scaled_centroids([[h * 10, l] for h, l in X], y), [[h * 10, l] for h, l in new])
assert cm == mm, f'centimetres {cm} vs millimetres {mm}: standardized values have no units'
assert cm[0] == 'fern', f'(20.6, 2.5) is a fern once both features count; got {cm}'

tests.name: tiny units don't matter either
tests.code:
X = [[12.0, 3.1], [14.5, 2.8], [13.3, 3.6], [16.8, 4.4], [30.2, 4.5], [28.4, 5.1], [26.0, 4.2], [22.5, 5.0]]
y = ['fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm']
new = [[20.6, 2.5], [15.0, 5.2], [27.0, 3.0], [21.0, 4.0]]
cm = predict_scaled(fit_scaled_centroids(X, y), new)
tiny = fit_scaled_centroids([[h * 1e-12, l] for h, l in X], y)
assert abs(tiny['stds'][0] / fit_scaled_centroids(X, y)['stds'][0] - 1e-12) < 1e-21, f'the stored spread shrinks with the unit, it does not become 1; got {tiny["stds"]}'
assert predict_scaled(tiny, [[h * 1e-12, l] for h, l in new]) == cm, 'heights in units a trillion times larger give the same predictions'

tests.name: a single new example
tests.code:
X = [[12.0, 3.1], [14.5, 2.8], [13.3, 3.6], [16.8, 4.4], [30.2, 4.5], [28.4, 5.1], [26.0, 4.2], [22.5, 5.0]]
y = ['fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm']
model = fit_scaled_centroids(X, y)
assert predict_scaled(model, [[20.6, 2.5]]) == ['fern'], 'one row has no spread of its own: scale it with the stored statistics'
assert predict_scaled(model, [[29.0, 5.0]]) == ['palm']

tests.name: prediction uses the stored statistics
ties go to the first label in sorted order
tests.code:
model = {'means': [0.0, 0.0], 'stds': [1.0, 1.0], 'centroids': {'b': [0.0, 0.0], 'a': [2.0, 0.0]}}
assert predict_scaled(model, [[1, 0]]) == ['a'], 'equally near a and b: choose a'

tests.name: near the boundary, nothing is rounded
no rows to predict
tests.code:
X = [[12.0, 3.1], [14.5, 2.8], [13.3, 3.6], [16.8, 4.4], [30.2, 4.5], [28.4, 5.1], [26.0, 4.2], [22.5, 5.0]]
y = ['fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'fern', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm', 'palm']
model = fit_scaled_centroids(X, y)
assert predict_scaled(model, []) == [], 'predicting no rows gives an empty list'

tests.name: three classes
tests.code:
model = fit_scaled_centroids([[0], [1], [10], [11], [20], [21]], ['c', 'c', 'a', 'a', 'b', 'b'])
assert sorted(model['centroids']) == ['a', 'b', 'c']
got = predict_scaled(model, [[0.4], [10.6], [20.2], [30]])
assert got == ['c', 'a', 'b', 'b'], f'every class can be predicted, including the last in sorted order; got {got}'

tests.name: a constant feature
tests.code:
model = fit_scaled_centroids([[1, 5], [2, 5], [9, 5], [10, 5]], ['lo', 'lo', 'hi', 'hi'])
assert model['stds'][1] == 1.0 and model['means'][1] == 5.0, f'spread 0 is replaced by 1; got {model}'
assert predict_scaled(model, [[3, 5], [8, 5]]) == ['lo', 'hi']

tests.name: every feature counts
tests.code:
model = fit_scaled_centroids([[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 1], [0, 0, 9], [0, 0, 10]], ['p', 'p', 'q', 'q'])
assert predict_scaled(model, [[0, 0, 7], [0, 0, 2]]) == ['q', 'p'], 'the third feature decides'

tests.name: bad input

questions.prompt: A feature has training mean 50 and standard deviation 5. What is the standardized value of 60?
Where should the means and standard deviations used to scale the test set come from?
choices: Each test row on its own
questions.explanation: They are learned parameters: fit on training data, then reuse them unchanged.

questions.prompt: Every training example has the same value, 7, in one feature. What does this lesson's scaler do with that feature?
questions.explanation: Its spread is 0, so the lesson divides by 1 after subtracting the mean 7, leaving 0 everywhere.

questions.prompt: After standardizing, you convert one feature from metres to centimetres and standardize again. Do nearest-centroid predictions change?
choices: No: standardized values have no units
Yes: every value is 100 times larger
Only if the feature is constant
questions.explanation: Multiplying a feature by 100 multiplies its mean and spread by 100 too, so the standardized values are identical.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Explain why features with large ranges or arbitrary units dominate distance-based models.
- Standardize features column by column with NumPy broadcasting.
- Learn scaling statistics from training data only and reuse them for new examples.
- Build a classifier whose predictions don't depend on the units of its features.
